God is Jabbar (the Compeller) and you may be a compeller; God is Ghani (the Self-Sufficient) and you may be rich; is your richness like the richness of God? God has action and you have action; is your action like the action of God?

So there is a difference between essential attributes and bestowed attributes, which the Giver withdraws whenever He wills.

Subhan Allah may also be said to express wonder. When you hear a strange statement, you say: "Subhan Allah," meaning: I exalt God above such a statement having occurred.

Thus they say here, "Subhanaka" (25:18): meaning, it is strange that we should lead astray, how could we, who worship You, make others worship us? The meaning is that this is not valid from us. How could we, who call people to worship You, then turn around and have them worship us? It is not reasonable that we would call them to worship You and then become those whom they worship: "Glory be to You, it was not for us to take any protectors besides You" (25:18).

You are our Protector, the One we draw near to, and You have sent us on a mission, and Your right choice of us must prevent us from doing this; otherwise we would not have been trustworthy in this mission. So "Subhanaka" means: exalting You from choosing one who is not worthy of the mission, so that he takes the matter for himself.

The meaning of "ma kana yanbaghi lana" (it was not for us) (25:18) is the negation of propriety. We say: "It is not becoming (ma yanbaghi) for so-and-so to do such-and-such," as God Most High said concerning His Messenger ﷺ: "We did not teach him poetry, nor is it becoming for him" (36:69). Poetry is a faculty and a gift of eloquent expression, and the Arabs prided themselves on this gift; if a poet arose among them, they took pride in him and his standing was raised. This faculty was available to the Messenger of God.

Had the Prophet ﷺ been a poet, he would have been a creative poet, but it was not becoming for him to be so, because poetry is based on imagination. Therefore God kept him far from poetry, so that the people would not think that what Muhammad brought of the Qur'an was the imaginings of a poet. The nature of the Messenger of God was not rigid or unfit for poetry; rather, he ﷺ had a refined sensibility, and had it been decreed for him to be a poet, he would have been great.

The Truthful, glorified and exalted, has said concerning the poets:

"And the poets—the erring follow them. Do you not see that they wander in every valley, and that they say what they do not do?" (26:224-226).

They have also said about poetry: "Its sweetest is its most false," so the Prophet ﷺ never entered this field throughout his life.

Thus their saying, "Subhanaka" (25:18), is a response to "Did you lead astray these, My servants, or did they themselves stray from the way?" (25:17). Then he mentions the proof of "Or did they themselves stray from the way?" (25:17) in His saying: "But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the Reminder, and they were a people doomed to ruin" (25:18). So when You gave them enjoyment, O Lord, You made them affluent in luxury, and blessing preoccupied them from the Blesser, so they deviated from the path.

The verse alerts the believer not to grieve over a blessing he has lost, for this blessing may tempt you and divert you from the Blesser, Mighty and Majestic. Therefore it is better that God withholds it from you, because you cannot guarantee yourself in a state of blessing.

His saying, Most High: "until they forgot the Reminder" (25:18): meaning, they forgot the Blesser. The right of a blessing is not to forget the Blesser. Therefore we have said that if health is a blessing from the Glorified, then the sick person who is deprived of it is not out of the Blesser's blessing; rather, he is in His companionship and presence.

From here, when one of the knowers of God fell ill, he would become angry when prayed for to be cured, and would say to his visitor: "Do not cut off my intimacy with my Lord."

There is a hadith qudsi: "O son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit Me." He said: "How could I visit You, when You are the Lord of the worlds?" He said: "Did you not know that My servant so-and-so was sick and you did not visit him? Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him." (1)

So when the sick person knows that he is in God's company, he is ashamed to despair.

The meaning of "a people doomed to ruin" (25:18): al-bur means destruction, and from it comes "barren land" (ard bur), which is land that does not grow anything.

1 Narrated by Muslim in his Sahih (2569), Book of Righteousness and Kinship, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 25, verse 19:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿So they have indeed denied you in what you say, so you cannot avert (the punishment) nor obtain help. And whoever among you wrongs, We will make him taste a great punishment.﴾

After Allah—blessed and exalted is He, and He knows them best—asked them: ﴿Did you mislead these, My servants, or did they stray from the way themselves?﴾ (25:17), and they answered: ﴿But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the remembrance, and they were a people ruined.﴾ (25:18), this question shook them with a severe jolt. He, glory be to Him, wished to absolve them, so He said: ﴿So they have indeed denied you in what you say…﴾ (25:19). That is: I know that you spoke the truth, but they denied you in what you say. ﴿…so you cannot avert (the punishment) nor obtain help…﴾ (25:19). Then He turned to them.

Sarf (ṣarf, turning away/averting) means that you repel by your own self the evil that someone might direct at you, and naṣr (help) means that when you yourself cannot repel it from yourself, someone comes to repel it for you.

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And whoever among you wrongs, We will make him taste a great punishment.﴾ (25:19). Someone may ask: why does the Truth, glory be to Him, address His friends with this harshness? They say: in reality this harshness is not a rebuke to the friends of Allah; rather it is a warning and a call to attention for others. If the Truth, glory be to Him, addresses those who obey Him with this harshness, then what of His enemies and those who rebel against His method?

When they hear this address, they must say: although Allah chose them and brought them near, that did not prevent Him from directing them to the truth and rebuking them.

Did He not say, glory be to Him, about His beloved and Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And if he had attributed to Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ (69:44–46)? So the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, speaks of His Prophet in this manner in order to frighten and intimidate others.

Ẓulm (wrongdoing) is taking the right of another. Since Allah, exalted is He, has forbidden that, this means that Allah wants every person to enjoy the fruit of his own effort, because the affairs of life do not stand straight if a person takes the fruit of another and becomes accustomed to living on the blood and sweat of others. Therefore we see in society some criminals and deviants (who have lost their way) who live on the sweat of others while they themselves do not sweat.

When a person's right is taken from its owner and he finds no one to do him justice and restore his stolen right, he inclines to laziness and turns away from work and exertion. It is well known that the fruit of work does not return only to its doer, but also to others, since it facilitates people's interests and contributes by its movement to the movement of society.

We have said before that the difference between the believer and others in work is that the disbeliever works for himself, whereas the believer works for what suffices him and strives to help others. Therefore you should work according to your capacity, not according to your need, for your need is met by what you achieve with your effort, and what remains is for those who cannot work and have no capacity.

As for the struggle between the disbelievers and the believers, led by the messengers, Allah, exalted is He, decides it. He says: no one of My creatures can wrong Me, because the one wronged has a point of weakness, and the wrongdoer has a point of strength. Therefore He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ (2:57). That is: no one is able to do that. ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾ (2:57): so their wrong was to themselves, not to the believers.

The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, is jealous for His servant lest he wrong himself, because a human being has several faculties: the faculty of seeking immediate gratification and the faculty of deferred deliberation. The diligent student chose deferred comfort, and the lazy one chose immediate comfort. Both love themselves and seek its comfort, but there is a difference between conscious love and foolish love. The first endures hardships to attain in the end the highest ranks, while the other is lured by immediate comfort, and soon finds himself a vagabond in society. The enjoyment of the first is more lasting and longer, and the enjoyment of the other is quick and ends.

This is a general rule said of the work of this world and said of the work of the Hereafter. The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, created the human being and loves that one faculty in the soul not wrong another faculty, and that the faculty of haste not wrong the faculty of deliberation; for the faculty of haste takes a quick good that ends, whereas the faculty of deliberation attains the lasting good that does not end.

So Allah, exalted is He, wants His creation, whether believer or disbeliever, not to wrong themselves, because Allah honored him, created the whole universe for his service, and subjected it for his sake. Therefore He says to him: you cannot wrong Me, nor wrong the believers; you only wrong yourself. So a Lord who punishes a person for having wronged himself is indeed a good Lord.

Therefore it has come in the sacred hadith: "O son of Adam, I love you—as evidence, I punish you if you wrong yourself—so by My right over you, be lovers of Me." (2)

As for the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, magnifying the punishment: ﴿And whoever among you wrongs, We will make him taste a great punishment.﴾ (25:19), it is only so that He may make His servants shun it and keep them away from its causes, so that it does not occur.

Often the enemies of Islam raise objections to His saying: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion…﴾ (2:256). They say: then why do you kill whoever apostatizes from Islam? They do not realize that this ruling is a barrier placed in the path of everyone who wishes to believe, and a warning to him so that he thinks carefully about what he is about to undertake if he chooses Islam; so he does not enter it except after consent and complete conviction. When he knows this ruling, he takes precautions in the matter, and enters it by his own free choice and reasoned judgment.

Islam does not want a hasty multitude; rather it wants deliberation, reason and reflection. This counts in Islam's favor, not against it. It is like a precious commodity whose owner is confident of its quality, just as you go to a cloth merchant, for example, and he displays his goods to you, shows you their quality and tests them before you. Why? Because he is confident in the quality of his merchandise.

Among this is what many verses of the Wise Reminder end with, such as: "do you reflect," "do you reason," "do you remember." This is evidence that if you reason, if you reflect, if you remember, you would be guided to what the Qur'an brought.

So His saying: ﴿And whoever among you wrongs, We will make him taste a great punishment﴾ (25:19): what might be objected to the Qur'an, or to the Truth, glory be to Him, is that the wrongdoer, when he wrongs, is punished for himself, since something was taken from him. But the Truth, glory be to Him, took nothing from him; rather He, with the attributes of perfection in Him, created you, so you wronged only yourselves.

1 Al-Waatin: a vein in the heart; if it is severed, its owner dies. It is the main vital artery that supplies the body with pure blood coming out of the heart. Allah says: ﴿Then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ (69:46), meaning: We would have ended his life swiftly and destroyed him quickly if he opposed Our command in any way. (Al-Qamus al-Qawmi, 2/219).

2 Imam Abu Hamid al-Ghazali cited it in *Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din* (4/296), saying: "In some books: My servant, I am your lover, and by My right over you, be lovers of Me."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 25, verse 20:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says concerning His messengers and prophets:

﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they surely ate food and walked in the markets. And We have made some of you a trial for others. Will you be patient? And your Lord is ever Seeing.﴾

We have already spoken on His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "What is this messenger that eats food and walks in the markets...?"﴾ (al-Furqan 7). This is the attribute of all the messengers, and Muhammad was not an innovation in that. If eating food were to detract from his being a messenger, ﷺ, and they wanted a messenger who does not eat food, then we say: By Allah, if eating food prevented him, in your view, from being a messenger, then how do you say of one who ate food that he is a god? How, when you yourselves did not accept him as a messenger?

Blessed and exalted is Allah, who made the messengers eat food and walk in the markets, because the messenger must be a model and exemplar in everything for creation. For this reason the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was at the lowest level of material conditions of the world in matters of worldly affairs: food, drink and clothing. This was so that he would be an example for people. Likewise we find him ﷺ eager that his household be like him, and therefore he did not give them a share in zakat, which those like them among the poor take.

The Prophet ﷺ says: "We, the company of prophets, do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity" (1).

And whoever among the Muslims had a debt, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would bear it on his behalf. All of this, if it indicates anything, indicates that he ﷺ was certain of the reward of the Hereafter, so that nothing of worldly things should be required of him.

For this reason we have said: If you look at the principles of truth and the principles of falsehood before you in this world, you will find that the principle of falsehood pays its price first. For example, in order to be a communist you must take the price first. As for the principle of truth, you pay the price in advance: you tire, are wronged, tortured, hungry and made homeless, and you leave your family and your wealth, then you await the reward in the Hereafter. By this measure you can distinguish between truth and falsehood.

As for His words, ﴿and walk in the markets...﴾ (al-Furqan 20): that is, they frequent them to attend to their needs and buy their requirements, which is evidence of their humility and their not being proud toward such tasks. For this reason our master, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, would carry his own needs himself, and if one of his companions offered to carry them for him, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would say: "The owner of a thing has more right to carry it" (2).

As for the meaning of ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others. Will you be patient?...﴾ (al-Furqan 20): which "some" is a trial for which "some"? As in His words: ﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees...﴾ (al-Zukhruf 32): that is, which "some" is raised, and over which "some" is it raised?

We observe in such matters that people look only at one angle: this one is rich and that one is poor. But if they were to weigh people by all aspects of the human soul, they would find that in every person there is a gift which Allah has specially granted him. Each of us has a distinction that his brother does not have. That is so that people may support one another and creation may complete itself. For if the world were one identical copy repeated, no one would need anyone, and no one would ask about anyone. But when gifts are many, you have what I do not have, and society is bound together by mutual need, not by mere favour.

Suppose that all people graduated from university and became (doctors). Then who would sweep the street? At that point one of us would volunteer for this task one day. Thus need becomes the daughter of volunteering and favour, and favour obliges no one to work, so affairs would be disrupted. But when need calls you, it is you who hastens to the work and seeks it out.

Do you not see those in arduous professions going out in the morning seeking work, and one of them becoming angry if he does not find an opportunity for work on his day, with what he bears of pain and hardship? Why? It is need.

So the worker who works in sewers, for example, and bears their harm, is, in his capacity over himself and his contentment with the decree of Allah concerning him, better than I am in this matter, because I am not able for this work and he is able for it. Had Allah left such work to voluntary favour, no one would have undertaken it. Thus, the subjugations (of some to others) come from Allah, glory be to Him, for a wisdom.

Such arduous works, or those that harm the worker, are regarded by some as base occupations, and this is an error. Any work that benefits society is not base; there is no base work at all, only a base worker.

So the meaning of ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others...﴾ (al-Furqan 20) is that each of us is a trial for the other. The rich man is a trial for the poor, and the poor man is a trial for the rich, and so on. When the rich man exalts himself over the poor and humiliates him, the poor man here is a trial for the rich. When the poor man resents the rich man and envies him, the rich man here is a trial for the poor. Likewise the healthy is a trial for the sick, and the messengers are a trial for those who denied them, and the disbelievers are a trial for the messengers.

People flee from trial in itself, and this is not correct, because trial means testing. What one should flee from is the outcome of the trial, not the trial itself. The examination is a trial for students: whoever succeeds, the trial is good for him, and whoever fails, the trial is evil for him. Therefore trial in itself is not blameworthy.

For this reason the word "fitna" is taken from the smelting of gold, and it is known that gold is the best of metals, even if something more precious is found. Why? Because among its qualities it does not oxidise and does not react with others, and it is also easy to cast. Therefore they say: "The precious metal is like the good: slow to break, quick to mend." For example, when gold breaks it is easy to restore and fashion again, unlike glass, for instance.

So trial is a test, and the skilful is the one who succeeds in it. If one is rich, he is thankful, fulfils the right of wealth, is humble, seeks out the poor and shows compassion to them. And the poor is the one unable to earn, not the poor man who has taken up thuggery and devoured people's wealth by falsehood.

Since trial requires patience from the one tried, He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Will you be patient?﴾ (al-Furqan 20). So every trial needs patience. Will you be patient through it?

And because of the importance of patience, Allah, exalted is He, says in Surat al-'Asr: ﴿By time, indeed mankind is in loss, except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience﴾ (al-'Asr 1-3). That is: mankind in general is in loss, and nothing saves him from it except that he possess these qualities.

The verse concludes with His words, glory be to Him: ﴿And your Lord is ever Seeing﴾ (al-Furqan 20): to alert us that every movement of yours within trial is seen by Us, and Our seeing of deeds is not merely for knowledge, but so that We may award a recompense for them in accordance with them.

(1) Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (2/463) with the wording: "We, the company of prophets, do not leave inheritance; what I leave after the maintenance of my worker and the provision of my wives is charity," from the hadith of Abu Hurairah. Also narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (4033), Kitab al-Maghazi, from the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab, and likewise by Muslim in his Sahih, Kitab al-Jihad.

(2) Cited by al-Haythami in Majma' al-Zawa'id (5/122) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah, and he said: "Narrated by Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and in its chain is Yusuf ibn Ziyad al-Basri, who is weak." Al-'Ajluni said in Kashf al-Khafa' (2/25): "Al-Qadi 'Iyad mentioned it in al-Shifa' without attribution, and it is weak; indeed Ibn al-Jawzi exaggerated and listed it among the fabricated (hadiths)," and Mulla 'Ali al-Qari disagreed with him in al-Asrar al-Marfu'ah (hadith 553).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 25, verse 21:

Then He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say, "Why were the angels not sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?" Indeed, they have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great insolence.﴾

Al-liqa' (the meeting) means the resurrection (al-ba'th). We believed in Allah in the unseen, and in the Hereafter we will believe in Him, exalted is He, as witnessed: ﴿"To whom belongs the dominion today?..."﴾ (Ghafir 16). Even one who did not believe in this world will believe in the Hereafter.

Therefore He, glory be to Him, says in another place: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain, which the thirsty one thinks is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing; and he finds Allah with him, and He pays him his account in full. And Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ (al-Nur 39).

Would that he had come and not found his deed! The calamity is that he finds his deed complete, and finds Allah calling him to account and recompensing him, and all of this was not on his mind in the world; therefore he is surprised by it now.

His saying: ﴿Those who do not expect to meet Us...﴾ (al-Furqan 21) means: they do not await it, nor do they believe in it; therefore they did not prepare for it. Why? Because they preferred the comfort of the immediate over the comfort of the final, and they saw before them desires and pleasures they did not have patience for, and they neglected the ultimate end.

What is the liqa'? Liqa' means connection and encounter. But how does the connection and encounter take place between the Real, blessed and exalted, and the creation? This is among the matters over which much disputation has occurred, and about which a commotion arose that caused Muslims to doubt in many questions.

Some said: liqa' requires that Allah be embodied, and this is prohibited. Others said: it is not necessary that liqa' be a connection; it may be merely seeing, since the eye's seeing of the Lord is not a meeting. This is the saying of the People of the Sunna.

As for the Mu'tazila, they denied even seeing, and said: they do not meet Him in connection or in seeing, because the one who sees delimits the seen, and this is impossible for Allah, mighty and majestic.

We say to the Mu'tazila: you take matters concerning Allah in the same way you take them concerning Allah's creatures. Why do you not take everything concerning Allah within the framework of ﴿There is nothing like Him﴾ (al-Shura 11)? If for you there is a meeting that requires connection, then for Allah there is a meeting that does not require connection; and if seeing delimits, then for Allah there is a seeing that does not delimit. You have a hearing, and Allah has hearing; does your hearing equal the hearing of Allah, mighty and majestic? Then why do you want the meeting with Allah to be like your meeting, requiring embodiment, or His seeing to be like your seeing?

Therefore, in the story of Musa's seeing of his Lord, mighty and majestic, what did Musa say? He said: ﴿"My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look upon You..."﴾ (al-A'raf 143). He asked his Lord to show Him, because he could not do that by his own essence, and was not fit for this seeing, unless Allah showed Himself and made him perceive. The matter is not on the side of the seen, but on the side of the seer. But did Allah rebuke him for this request and say of him: he was arrogant and transgressed with great insolence, as He says here? No; He said to him: ﴿"You will not see Me..."﴾ (al-A'raf 143). He did not say, "I will not be seen," and there is a difference between the two expressions.

His saying: ﴿"You will not see Me..."﴾ (al-A'raf 143) means: are you stronger, or the mountain? ﴿So when his Lord revealed Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble, and Musa fell down unconscious...﴾ (al-A'raf 143).

Note: ﴿When his Lord revealed Himself to the mountain...﴾ (al-A'raf 143). The word tajalla (revealed Himself) means that Allah, exalted is He, manifests Himself to some of His creatures. But can they endure this manifestation? The mountain is not more honored with Allah than man, for whom Allah subjected the mountain and everything in existence.

So man is the more honored, but his constitution and nature are not fit for this seeing, and he does not have the readiness to receive the divine lights, because Allah created him for the earth. In the Hereafter, however, the matter is different; therefore Allah will alter this creation so that its realities change and it becomes able to see. If Musa, peace be upon him, fell unconscious at the seeing of the one manifested to him, which was the mountain, how then would it be if he saw the One manifested, mighty and majestic?

Therefore, among Allah's blessings upon His servants in the Hereafter is: ﴿Faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ (al-Qiyama 22-23).

And He said of the disbelievers: ﴿Nay, indeed they will be veiled from their Lord that day﴾ (al-Mutaffifin 15). So what distinguishes the believers from the disbelievers is that they will not be veiled from seeing their Lord, mighty and majestic, after their otherworldly constitution has changed, and they become able to see what they did not see in the world. And if people today, with the advance of knowledge, make for the weak-sighted things that increase their sight and vision, why do we deem this unlikely with regard to Allah?

Therefore, you find those who are immoderate toward themselves arguing with you in what comforts them: you see them denying the resurrection and keeping this idea far from themselves, because they know the evil of their end if they were certain of the resurrection and acknowledged it.

Among those immoderate toward themselves are even some who believe in a god. One of them says: since Allah has decreed disobedience upon me, why does He hold me accountable for it? We are astonished, because they do not mention the counterpart and do not say: since He has decreed obedience upon us, why does He reward us for it? So they did not stand the sound rational stance; the first is what would draw evil upon them, so they mentioned it, while the other is good coming to them, so they neglected to mention it.

Their saying: ﴿Why were the angels not sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?﴾ (al-Furqan 21) indicates their arrogance and their objection to the Messenger being a human. In another place they said: ﴿Shall mere humans guide us?﴾ (al-Taghabun 6).

So everything that angers them is that the Messenger should be a human, and this objection shows their foolishness. If the Messenger had come as an angel, he could not have been a model for them. The Messenger came only to be a model, a teacher of the method, and an exemplar of conduct. Had he come as an angel, he could indeed have taught us Allah's method, but he could not be a model of conduct for us. If he commanded you to do something while being an angel, you would have the right to object and say: you are an angel, you are able to do that, but I am a human who is not able to.

So the Real, glory be to Him, says: note that the messengers have two tasks: the task of delivering the message and the task of being a behavioral exemplar. If they had been of a nature other than human, the delivery would have been possible for them, but it would not be possible for them to be a model and a pattern to be followed.

And if the Messenger had come as an angel in his true form, you would not have seen him, and you would not have needed him in a human form; and then you would not know whether he is an angel or a human. Therefore the matter must return to his being a human. Hence He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have confused them as they are confusing [themselves]﴾ (al-An'am 9).

As for the descent of angels with the Messenger, it is among the proposals the disbelievers put to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, to ask of his Lord. This means they want a sign of confirmation for the prophethood of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. The Messenger of Allah had already come to them with a miracle of the kind in which they excelled and in which they were unable to compete with him, to establish that it came from their mighty Lord. The meaning of this miracle is that it stands in place of His saying: "My servant has spoken the truth in everything he conveys from Me." And since the miracle has come attesting to the Messenger, is there any miracle greater than a miracle?

The miracle of the Qur'an has been sufficient to stand as proof of the Messenger's truthfulness in conveying from Allah. Moreover, it has brought you unseen matters that no human can know, neither of the past that happened before he was born, nor of the future that will happen after he is born.

So the proof of the Messenger's truthfulness is established. What, then, has moved you to propose other miracles?

Their saying: ﴿or [why do] we [not] see our Lord?﴾ (al-Furqan 21): By Allah, if there were a god who could be seen by you, he would not be fit to be a god; for what is seen is encompassed by the pupil of the seer, and whatever encompasses it is limited, and its limitedness contradicts its divinity.

Otherwise, the meanings that stir the human soul, such as the truth and justice that people speak of, call for, fanatically defend, and rush toward to solve their problems and ease their lives: do you perceive these meanings and their like by the senses? How, then, do you ask to perceive their Creator, mighty and majestic, by the senses?

Therefore the Real, glory be to Him, concludes this matter with His saying: ﴿Indeed, they have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great insolence.﴾ (al-Furqan 21). Istakbara and takabbara: he tried to make himself above his measure, and each of us has a limited measure.

Hence the transmitted saying: "May Allah have mercy on the man who knows his own measure." Why, then, does a human become arrogant? If you are a sound human, you are pleased when we prevent from you someone who would steal from you, or look at your womenfolk, or wrong you; so why do you become angry when we prevent you from the like of this?

The rational view is that you compare what is yours with what is upon you. We have prevented your hand, which is one, from stealing; in exchange, we have prevented all people's hands from stealing from you, we have prevented your eye from reaching toward others' womenfolk, and we have prevented all eyes from reaching toward your womenfolk. Why, then, do you rejoice at this and become angry at that? You ought to judge by the same logic: if you love what is yours and hate what is another's, you have departed from the right and opposed justice.

Among their arrogance was their confrontation with the Messenger of Allah at the start of his call, when they said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from one of the two cities?﴾ (al-Zukhruf 31). So the Qur'an is beyond reproach, and this was a realistic judgment on their part, since they were a people of eloquence and rhetoric, and the Qur'an is at the highest level of eloquence and clarity. What stuck in their throats was that the Messenger should be a man of common people; they wanted him to be great in their eyes, so that when they followed him he would have a standing that calls for following him.

So arrogance is that you are too proud to be a follower of one whom you see as beneath you. We deny this, because you did not see Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, as beneath you in carrying the message; rather, you placed him at the highest rank and called him "the truthful, the trustworthy." So when did you make him beneath you? It is the gift Allah bestowed upon him, the message that made you take from him what you used to give before he became a messenger.

Have you ever heard of a messenger whose Lord, mighty and majestic, came with him saying to his people: "This is My messenger"? And since Allah will confront you with this confrontation, there is no need then for a messenger, since Allah will address you directly with the obligation and the matter ends. It is known that this did not happen; you are asking for something you have never heard of, and this is evidence of your hesitancy and your arrogance in refusing to accept faith, so you have come up with something impossible.

So the matter, from the disbelievers, is hesitancy, obstinacy and arrogance in refusing to accept the clear truth. They had previously proposed similar signs and miracles, and when Allah answered them, they denied. Yet signs and miracles are not the proposal of those to whom the messenger is sent; they are a favor from Allah, mighty and majestic, the Giver of this message.

The root of istikbar is k-b-r, and it comes with several meanings: one says kabura yakburu, meaning he grew old in his age and size; and kabura yakburu, meaning he became great in his essence, and among its uses is His saying: ﴿Great is the word that comes out of their mouths...﴾ (al-Kahf 5).

Takabbara means he displayed the quality of greatness to people; istakbara means he does not have the qualifications of greatness, yet he seeks to be great.

So the meaning of ﴿they have become arrogant...﴾ (al-Furqan 21) is not in the reality of their constitution, but ﴿they have become arrogant within themselves...﴾ (al-Furqan 21): in that they follow the Messenger; that is, it is too great for them to be followers of a man whom they see as richer or better than them (by their own claim).

We see, for example, one of the local strongmen before whom everyone submits, yet when he sees one stronger than himself he shrinks before him and becomes humble; because he is arrogant without a basis, and in something not intrinsic to him... So the arrogant one without a basis is heedless of the greatness of his Lord, and if he sensed the greatness of Allah, mighty and majestic, he would be ashamed to be arrogant.

Therefore we see the people of obedience and knowledge always humble, why? Because they always sense the greatness of Allah. A person does not become tyrannical unless he sees everyone beneath him and there is none greater than him. A person should not be arrogant except by something intrinsic to him that cannot be stripped from him: if you are arrogant by your wealth, you may become poor; if you are arrogant by your strength, sickness may strike you; if you are arrogant by your knowledge, you cannot be sure it will not be taken from you, so that you come to know nothing after having known.

And among Allah's kindness and mercy toward creation is that greatness belongs to Him alone; and to Him alone, glory be to Him, belongs pride and majesty, and the Real, blessed and exalted, declares it: "Greatness is My cloak, and majesty is My garment; whoever contests Me in either..."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 25, verse 22:

Then the Truthful (al-Haqq), glory be to Him, says:

﴿On the Day they see the angels, there will be no glad tidings that Day for the guilty, and they will say, "A forbidding, forbidden barrier."﴾

The Truthful (al-Haqq), blessed and exalted is He, speaks of those who proposed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that signs be sent down, and who demanded that the angels descend with him so that they might see them and bear witness to his truthfulness (ﷺ). So He, glory be to Him, says to them: You wish to see the angels, so you will see them, but in another situation, not a situation of glad tidings and good things, but in a situation of disgrace, remorse and punishment: ﴿On the Day they see the angels, there will be no glad tidings that Day for the guilty...﴾ (al-Furqan 25:22).

So you will see them with the sight of terror when they come to take your souls, or you will see them on the Day of Resurrection, the Day they give you the tidings of punishment.

On the Day they meet the believers: ﴿Glad tidings to you today: gardens beneath which rivers flow...﴾ (al-Hadid 57:12). Then the disbelievers will strain to hear this word, but far is it (hayhat): ﴿there will be no glad tidings that Day for the guilty...﴾ (al-Furqan 25:22). They are denied this beloved word which they were awaiting, and they are met with another word that suits them.

They will say to them: ﴿A forbidding, forbidden barrier﴾ (al-Furqan 25:22). Al-hajr means prevention, and from it comes our saying "nahjur ʿala fulan" (we place someone under restraint), meaning we prevent him from disposing of his affairs. In former times they used to say, to ward off evil, "hijran mahjuran," meaning "a prohibition," and similar to this is what we hear them say when the jinn are mentioned: "ḥābis ḥābis," meaning: keep away from me, do not come near me.

Then the Exalted says:

﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust.﴾

When you look at non-believers, you find among them people who are fit for goodness and for doing what is right, and among them are those with fine natural dispositions, such as those who gathered in the Alliance of the Virtuous (ḥilf al-fuḍūl) to support the oppressed, and the people of generosity and feeding the needy. Among them was one who had a great tent (qubba), in whose shade the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sheltered on a day of scorching heat. This means it was large, wide, set up and firm like a building, and from it they would feed the poor and the needy, and even the birds and the wild beasts. To this day we still cite Hatim al-Ta'i as the proverb for generosity. Among them were those who maintained family ties and relieved the distressed... etc.

But these and their like worked for the worldly station (jāh al-dunya), and God was not in their minds, whose pleasure they seek. The worker takes his reward from the one for whom he worked, as came in the sacred hadith: "You did it so that it would be said, and it has been said" (1).

And the Real, blessed and exalted is He, clarifies this matter in His saying, Exalted is He:
﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain, which the thirsty one thinks is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, and finds Allah with him, and He pays him his account in full. And Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ (al-Nur, 39)

And He, Exalted, also says:
﴿Their deeds are like ashes, which the wind blows hard on a stormy day...﴾ (Ibrahim, 18)

These people did many good deeds, but God was not in their minds; rather, they worked for humanity, for desire, and so that they would be spoken of. Therefore we see them in comfort and ease of living, enjoying all kinds of bliss. Why? Because they took the created causes that God Exalted created and carried them out precisely. God, blessed and exalted, does not deprive His servant of the fruit of his effort even if he is a disbeliever, while if a servant abandons the causes and is lazy, God deprives him even if he is a believer. There is a difference between the gifts of lordship (rubūbiyya), which encompass the believer and the disbeliever, the obedient and the disobedient, and the gifts of divinity (ulūhiyya).

Among the disbelievers are those who excelled in taking the causes, so they invented things that benefited humanity, and medicines that treated many diseases. Their reward must be given for this good, and they received their reward in this world as remembrance, honor, and perpetuation of their memory: statues were made for them, they were given medals, and books were written about their lives, as though God had not denied them their deed or diminished their right.

Do you not see that Abu Lahab, who took a hostile stance toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until there was revealed the saying of God, Exalted:
﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he. His wealth and what he earned will not avail him.﴾ (al-Masad, 1-2)
Yet despite this, God lightens his punishment, because he freed his slave-woman Thuwayba when she brought him the good news of the birth of Muhammad ibn Abd Allah, since he rejoiced at this news and was made happy by this report (2).

It is strange that these people stop at the crafts of men, which are nothing more than luxury in life, and so they record them and their makers in history, and forget the Creator of the necessities that helped them advance to the refinements and luxuries of life.

As for the word ﴿هباء﴾ (hab'a, "dust") in ﴿...hab'an (dust)...﴾ (al-Furqan, 23): things become apparent to a person either because their size is large or because they are near. If they are small in size, their sight is difficult. For example, you can see a bird or a sparrow if it flies in front of you, or even a hornet or a bee, but if a gnat flies in front of you, you cannot see it.

So: a thing disappears from sight because it is small in make-up, and the eye cannot perceive it; therefore they invented microscopes and telescopes.

A thing may also be far from you so that you do not see it because of its distance from the cone of light, since light begins from a point and then expands gradually in the shape of a cone, as when you look through a keyhole whose diameter is one centimetre, you can see an area much wider than it.

So: if you want to see the small, you magnify it, and if you want to see the distant, you bring it near.

And the hab' (ḥabā') is the particles that you see in the cone of light when it enters your room, which you do not see with the naked eye because of their fineness. This hab' that you see in the light is ﴿scattered dust﴾ (al-Furqan, 23): meaning, you cannot gather it, because it is dispersed and not stable; however much you stop the movement of the air, you find it moving in the light because of its small size.

If you say: we see them now making filters to trap this dust, so you gather it and purify the air of it, and these are shaped like sponge pores to which the dust clings, so it can be gathered.

We say: even with these filters, they collect only according to the fineness of the pores, and they trap only according to their capacity. Suppose you gathered it in this filter, then emptied it and said to me: this is the dust. We say to you: can you return each particle of it to its origin from which it flew?

1 Related by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad (2/322), and Muslim in his Sahih (1905), and al-Nasa'i in his Sunan (6/23-24), from the hadith of Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The first of people to be judged on the Day of Resurrection will be a man who was martyred. He will be brought forth and be made to recognize His blessings, and he will recognize them. He will be asked: What did you do with them? He will say: I fought for You until I was martyred. He will say: You lie, but you fought so that it would be said, 'He is brave,' and it has been said. Then he will be ordered, and he will be dragged on his face until he is thrown into the Fire." The hadith in full...

2 Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in al-Isaba fi Tamyiz al-Sahaba (8/36): "Ibn Sa'd said: al-Waqidi informed us, from more than one person of knowledge, who said: Thuwayba was the wet-nurse of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); he kept in touch with her while he was in Makkah, and Khadija would honor her, and she was in the possession of Abu Lahab, and [Khadija] asked him to sell her to her, but he refused. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) emigrated, Abu Lahab freed her, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to send her gifts and clothing until news came that she had died in the seventh year, on his return from Khaybar"...

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 25, verse 24:

﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day will have a better abode and a finer resting-place.﴾

After the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, described the outcome of the deeds of the disbelievers, He wished, glorified is He, to speak to us about the reward of the believers, following the Qur'an's custom of mentioning opposites which reveal one another. This mode of expression is abundant in the Book of God, among it: ﴿So let them laugh a little, and let them weep much...﴾ (al-Tawbah 82).

Among it also is the saying of the Truth, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss, and indeed, the wicked will be in Hellfire﴾ (al-Infitar 13-14).

Thus the Qur'an carries you from a thing to its opposite so that you may distinguish between them. The believer in bliss looks at the Fire and its heat, so he praises God who saved him from it; this is another blessing, greater than the first. And the disbeliever, when he looks at the bliss of the Garden, is filled with regret and knows the consequence of the disbelief that deprived him of this bliss, so this is more painful in its vexation and more severe in its punishment. Therefore they said: "Things are distinguished by their opposites."

As for His saying, glorified is He: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day will have a better abode and a finer resting-place﴾ (al-Furqan 24): "Companion" (sahib) of a thing is the one who accompanies it with love. So it is as if the Garden loves its people and they love it, for affection and companionship have arisen between them. Just as you love the place, the place loves you; and likewise, as you hate it, it hates you. From this is their saying: "nabā bihi al-makān," meaning: the place disliked him (rejected him).

And the phrase ﴿companions of the Garden...﴾ (al-Furqan 24) also indicates ownership, because they will not be brought out of it, and it will not cease or end.

And the word ﴿better...﴾ (al-Furqan 24): we have said that it is used in two ways. Khayr (good) is opposed by sharr (evil), as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ (al-Zalzalah 7-8), and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the best of creation﴾ (al-Bayyinah 6).

There is also khayr opposed by khayr, but lesser than it, as when you say: "This is better than that," and as in the noble hadith: "The strong believer is better and more beloved to God than the weak believer, and there is good in both" (1).

In some usages we do not suffice with the form (khayr) to distinguish between two things, so we say with the form of the comparative (af'al al-tafdil): "This is better than that" (akhyar min hadha).

As for the word ﴿resting-place (mustaqarr)...﴾ (al-Furqan 24): al-mustaqarr is the place in which you settle, and a person does not prefer settling in one place over another unless the place where he settles is more restful for himself than the other, as when we leave the room, for example, in the heat, and sit in the garden or the terrace.

From this we say: "If a land constrains you, leave it for another," in accordance with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever emigrates in the way of God will find in the earth many a refuge (2) and abundance...﴾ (al-Nisa' 100).

And the poet says: "By your life, no lands have constrained their people, but it is the characters of men that constrain."

As for the meaning of ﴿finer resting-place (ahsan maqilan)﴾ (al-Furqan 24): al-maqil is the place where the Arabs used to take the qaylulah (midday rest), which is the hour of noon when the sun's heat intensifies; in colloquial speech we call it (al-qayyala), and they say to one who does not rest at this hour: "The ghouls are resting!"

But is there a qaylulah in Paradise, when there is no heat, nor cold, nor freezing?

They said: qaylulah means the place of a person's leisure for his own self. Do you not see that the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, when He mentioned the times of seeking permission in Surah al-Nur, made this hour among them? He said, glorified is He: ﴿And when you lay aside your clothing at noon...﴾ (al-Nur 58). So He commanded the young ones to seek permission to come in upon us at this time, because it is one of the times of nakedness (awrah).

So: the mustaqarr is one thing, and the maqil for personal psychological rest is another thing, because you may settle in a place with others with you, whereas the maqil is a place specific to you. Thus, in the Garden you have two places: general and private. Therefore they said regarding the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ (al-Rahman 46): they said: a general garden and a private garden, just as you have a place for receiving guests and a place for yourself and your family.

(1) Related by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad (2/366-370), Muslim in his Sahih (2664), and Ibn Majah in his Sunan (79), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.

(2) That is: he finds a spacious place in which he may oppose (muraghamah) the people who opposed him and compelled him to emigrate, or finds a place suitable for opposing his enemies or guarding against their evil. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/270).

Al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66), on surah 25, verse 25:

The Truthful, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And the Day the sky is split open with clouds, and the angels are sent down in a descent.﴾

They had previously asked of Allah that angels be sent down to them. So here are the angels descending upon them as they wished, but not to your delight, nor as an answer to a request from you.

As for the sky (al-sama'): it is the raised ceiling above us, the guarded one that we look at, so we see in it no rifts (futur) nor cracks. You may look at the sky in its clarity, and you will find it smooth, with no protrusion in it, and no crookedness, despite its vastness and its standing thus without pillars.

For this reason the Truth, blessed and exalted, calls you to look and reflect. He says to you: We will not deceive you... Look at the sky and reflect: ﴿Then return the gaze twice; the gaze will return to you humbled while it is fatigued.﴾ (al-Mulk)

The sky that you see above you with this strength and cohesion, none holds it up above you except Allah, as He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; and if they should cease, none could hold them after Him...﴾ (Fatir, 41)

And He, exalted, says: ﴿And He holds the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission...﴾ (al-Hajj, 65). So: there is a permission for the sky to fall upon the earth, and to be split open and changed, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿On the Day the earth is replaced by other than the earth, and the heavens...﴾ (Ibrahim, 48).

And He, exalted, says about the splitting of the sky in the Hereafter: ﴿When the sky splits open, and it listens to its Lord and is made fit to do so.﴾ (al-Inshiqaq)

The meaning of ﴿and it listens to its Lord...﴾ (al-Inshiqaq, 2): that is, it hearkens and obeys merely upon hearing.

And here He, exalted, says: ﴿And the Day the sky is split open with clouds...﴾ (al-Furqan, 25): that is, it is split, and from its clefts the clouds descend. The cloud is also mentioned in His saying, exalted: ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of cloud, and the angels...﴾ (al-Baqarah, 210).

His saying, exalted: ﴿And the angels are sent down in a descent﴾ (al-Furqan, 25): indicates the intensity of the descent, so that they may take up the process of judgment at the station of the Resurrection.

Footnote 1: al-Futur: the cracks and fissures. Tafattara al-shay': it split. Al-Fatr: the split, plural futur. (Lisan al-'Arab, root f-t-r)

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 25, verse 26:

﴿The Sovereignty on that Day will be truly for the Most Merciful, and it will be a difficult day for the disbelievers.﴾

If in this world God, glory be to Him, lets some of His creation hold sovereignty over others, as He said, ﴿Say: O God, Possessor of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will...﴾ (Al 'Imran). We have said: there is a difference between al-mulk (possession, ownership) and al-mulk (kingship, rule). Al-milk is everything you possess, even the garment you wear is milk. As for al-mulk, it is that you hold authority over those who possess; this is what God, exalted is He, gives and bestows upon whom He wills from within His own sovereignty, as He gave it to the one who argued with His friend Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, because God had given him sovereignty...﴾ (Al-Baqarah). This is in this world. As for the Hereafter, there is no sovereignty and no possession for anyone, for all of this has been stripped away, and the sovereignty today belongs to God alone: ﴿Whose is the sovereignty today? It is God's, the One, the Subduer.﴾ (Ghafir).

So what is in your hand of the sovereignty of this world is an unstable sovereignty, which will quickly be taken from you. Therefore one of the knowers said to the caliph: "Had sovereignty remained with anyone else, it would not have reached you." The matter is not intrinsic to you; your sovereignty is from within the sovereignty of God, exalted is He, the Possessor, the True King. His sovereignty is firm and stable; it does not transfer nor cease.

And if ownership passes in this world from one person to another, it will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection into His hand, exalted is He. He gathers sovereignty and authority into one hand, which we dislike in this world, where we reject monopoly and dictatorship that places authority and oppression in one hand. If this is blameworthy among humans, it is praiseworthy with God, for in this world it is concentrated in the hand of one person with desires.

As for the Hereafter, it is in His hand, exalted is He. So mercy in this world is that sovereignty and authority be distributed, and mercy in the Hereafter is that it be gathered into His hand, exalted is He: ﴿The Sovereignty on that Day will be truly for the Most Merciful...﴾ (Al-Furqan). Therefore, the gathering of sovereignty to God on the Day of Resurrection is one of the manifestations of His mercy toward us. Do not take it as monopoly or tyranny, for it is in the hand of the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

It is as if the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, is reassuring you: do not worry, for on the Day of Resurrection the sovereignty does not belong to anyone whose dominion you fear to fall under; rather, "The Sovereignty on that Day will be truly for the Most Merciful."

Al-Haqq (the Truth): the thing that is established and does not change. Since it is established and does not change, it does not contradict or conflict. When a man speaks to you with words that have a reality in life and you ask him to repeat them, he repeats them a thousand times without altering anything. Why? Because he speaks from what he derives from the reality he has witnessed. But if he is lying, he derives nothing; therefore his speech must differ each time from the other. Hence they said: "If you are a liar, then be a good rememberer."

From His mercy, exalted is He, that He says: ﴿and it will be a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾ (Al-Furqan): He warns us of the danger before falling into it. This is mercy toward us, that our Lord advises us and makes things clear to us; otherwise, if He surprised us with punishment, the matter would be hard.

If you consider the opposite, He says it will be easy for the believers, so be keen, O human, to be among those who make it easy, not among those who make it hard for them.

¹ Hajjahu: he disputed with him over the proof; it is from the form of mufa'alah (reciprocal action) from both sides, meaning each of them presented his argument to overcome the other. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/143).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 25, verse 27:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And on the Day when the wrongdoer will bite on his hands, saying: "Oh, would that I had taken a way with the Messenger!"﴾

These are the days mentioned in these verses: ﴿On the Day they see the angels, there will be no good news that Day for the criminals...﴾ (22) (al-Furqan), and ﴿On the Day the wrongdoer will bite on his hands...﴾ (27) (al-Furqan). So the Day of Resurrection gathers all of this.

We have said that the wrongdoer (al-zalim) is the one who takes the right of another. Almighty and Exalted is He, clarifies this wrongdoing by His saying: ﴿And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves﴾ (2:57) (al-Baqarah).

For they are not able to wrong Allah, nor to wrong the Prophet (ﷺ). The word of Allah and His Messenger is the highest, and the religion of Allah will triumph in the end. Yet Allah punishes them for their wronging of themselves, and what a god is the God who does this to one who disobeys Him.

Even in the appearance of his wronging others, the disbeliever wrongs himself, because he places himself in the position of being responsible for these injustices. Therefore: if a person examines wrongdoing, he will find that it returns only to the wrongdoer himself.

When the wrongdoer sees the consequence of his wrongdoing, and witnesses the recompense of his deed, he bites on his hands in remorse and regret. Al-'add (biting) is the closing of the upper and lower jaws on something. Biting has stages that correspond to the distress to which a person resorts. In another place He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And when they are alone, they bite at you with their fingertips out of rage...﴾ (3:119) (Al 'Imran).

Al-anamil are the tips of the fingers, and biting them out of rage is a well-known habit when a person faces a situation in which it is hard for him to act; he bites his fingertips in a manner that suits the situation and the event. If the event is greater, it suits him to bite his hand upon his fingers alone; if it grows greater still, he bites both his hands together, as happens to them in the verse before us: ﴿And on the Day the wrongdoer will bite on his hands...﴾ (25:27) (al-Furqan), because he is in a state of regret and remorse over the opportunity that has passed him by and will not return, and the error that cannot be remedied. Therefore he torments himself before the punishment reaches him.

So he bites on both his hands together, as if the frightening matter he witnesses has reached its extreme. Therefore he bites his hands to reach the utmost in the thing bitten, for he is both the biter and the bitten. No one torments himself in this manner except one who has despaired of salvation.

Then He explains the cause of that: ﴿He will say: "Oh, would that I had taken a way with the Messenger!"﴾ (25:27) (al-Furqan). Although this verse was revealed concerning a particular event and a specific person, it encompasses everyone who does this. The lesson, as they say, is in the generality of the wording, not in the specificity of the cause. This is the recompense of every wrongdoer who swerves from the right path.

This verse was revealed concerning a particular event involving two men(1): 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, who was a generous man who fed people with food, and who once invited the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to his food. But the Messenger of Allah excused himself and said: "I cannot attend your food unless you bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." When the man bore witness to the two testimonies, the Messenger of Allah visited him and ate of his food. This angered Ubayy ibn Khalaf, 'Uqbah's companion, who said to him: "You have turned away (sabawta), O 'Uqbah!" 'Uqbah said: "By Allah, I only said that because I loved that Muhammad should eat at my place as people eat." Ubayy said: "Your image will not be cleared in my eyes unless you go to Muhammad in Dar al-Nadwa, step on his neck, and spit..." etc. 'Uqbah did what his companion advised him to do(2), and the verse was revealed: ﴿And on the Day the wrongdoer will bite on his hands, saying: "Oh, would that I had taken a way with the Messenger!"﴾ (25:27) (al-Furqan). The meaning of "the way" is his saying: there is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.

(1) Cited by al-Wahidi al-Naysaburi in Asbab al-Nuzul (p. 191). Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (2/317): "Whether its cause of revelation was 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt or another of the wretched, it is general to every wrongdoer."

(2) Al-Dahhak said: When 'Uqbah spat in the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), his spittle returned to his face and split into two parts, burning his cheeks, and the mark of that remained on him until death. Narrated by al-Wahidi in Asbab al-Nuzul (p. 192).

Then he says: ﴿Oh, woe to me! I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend.﴾

Al-Wayl (woe, ruin): destruction. He calls upon destruction and summons it to descend upon him. A person does not seek destruction for himself unless he is exposed to a punishment greater than destruction, as one of them said:

*Harder than the sickness that takes away sickness.*

And the words of the poet: "It is enough of a disease for you that you see death as a cure, and it suffices of deaths that they be hopes."(1)

Since the matter was greater than him and beyond his endurance, he called out, "Oh woe to me, come! This is your time, so that you may deliver me from the punishment I am in."

As for his saying ﴿I wish...﴾ (al-Furqan 28): it is tamanni (wishing), and tamanni is seeking something beloved that has no path to being attained, as the poet said in wishing: "Would that the stars would draw near to me so that I might string them into necklaces of praise; I would not be pleased with you for my speech."

And this is a matter that cannot be attained.

Another says: "Would that youth would return one day, so that I could tell it what old age has done."

The most that the wording of tamanni gives is that it indicates a beloved matter that one would like to happen; but will it actually happen? No.

The word *fulan* (so-and-so) is used as a euphemism for a person one dislikes, to the point that one does not even mention his name. So ʿUqba (ibn Abi Mu'ayt) did not say, "Would that I had not taken Umayya (ibn Khalaf) as a close friend," but said *fulanan* (so-and-so) because he hated him and detested even mentioning his name.

And *khalil* (close friend): from *khilla* and *mukhalla*, meaning the intertwined, mutual friendship. On this the poet says: "When we met, longing exerted its utmost; two close friends melting with anguish and reproach. He was a close friend within the closeness of his friend, and he vanished, slipping away amid the embrace."

(1) The verse is a well-known line of al-Mutanabbi (his Diwan 4/281), and Shihab al-Din Mahmud al-Halabi cited it in his book *Husn al-Tawassul ila Sina'at al-Tarassul* (252), in the section on "good openings."

Then he states the reason for that:

﴿He has led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me. And Satan is ever a deserter of man.﴾ [25:29]

﴿Khadhūlan⦆ (deserting, forsaking) is an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālaghah) of al-khidhlān (forsaking). One says khādhil and khadhūl. The meaning of "khadhalaka" is that he abandoned you in the matter after he had stretched out to you the ropes of hope. When the time of need for him arrives, he abandons you and leaves you. Likewise, Satan does this to his allies, as in other verses: ﴿Like Satan when he says to man, "Disbelieve." But when he disbelieves, [Satan] says, "Indeed, I am free of you. Indeed, I fear Allah, the Lord of the worlds."﴾ [59:16], and in another verse: ﴿And when Satan made their deeds appear pleasing to them and said, "No one can overcome you today from among the people, and indeed I am your protector..."﴾ [8:48].

In another place he says to his followers: ﴿I cannot help you, nor can you help me...﴾ [14:22]. So when they say to him, "You have led us astray and misguided us," he says to them: ﴿And I had over you no authority...﴾ [14:22], meaning: no authority of proof with which I persuaded you, nor any authority of coercion with which I compelled you and forced you to obey me. Rather, you were upon (tashwīrah) ﴿except that I invited you and you responded to me...﴾ [14:22].

¹ Al-Muṣrikh: the one who relieves and rescues the one who calls on him for help. Istaṣrakhahu: he sought help from him. Al-ṣarīkh: the cry for help, the one who seeks help, and the one who gives help. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/373)

Then the Almighty says about His Messenger, Muhammad (ﷺ):

﴿And the Messenger says: "My Lord, my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned."﴾ (25:30)

Al-qawm (the people): the people of a man are his family, his kinsfolk and those who live with him, and they are united either by a land or by a religion. They are called qawm because they are the ones who stand (yaqumun) over the affairs of things; so they are men specifically, because women are by nature expected to dwell and remain in the houses.

Allah, blessed and exalted, clarifies this distinction for us in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, let not a people (qawm) ridicule another people, perhaps they may be better than them; nor let women ridicule other women, perhaps they may be better than them...﴾ (49:11). So, qawm refers specifically to men.

Also among this is the saying of the poet(1):
"I do not know, and I do not think I know: are they the people (qawm) of Ḥiṣn, or women?" (2)

And His saying: ﴿My people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned﴾ (25:30). He attributed "the people" to Himself (ﷺ) because they are from him; they know him and know his origin, and they had testified to his truthfulness, trustworthiness and noble character before he was sent, and he was entrusted by them with their precious wealth. Therefore Allah, blessed and exalted, addressed them with His saying: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; grievous to him is what you suffer, concerned over you, to the believers gentle and merciful﴾ (9:128).

So, the Messenger is not distant from you, nor unknown to you; whoever does not believe in him as a messenger should believe in him as a model and exemplar of conduct, given his past history among you.

For this reason we see that our master Abu Bakr did not wait for a supplication from the Messenger of Allah, nor for him to recite Qur'an to him, nor to show him a miracle; rather he believed and affirmed the moment the Messenger of Allah spoke. Since he had said it, he had told the truth; it was not a miracle Abu Bakr saw, but rather his longstanding capital of knowledge of the Messenger of Allah in his conduct and character, for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would not abandon lying to people and then lie about the Creator.

Likewise Sayyida Khadija: did she wait for something from the Messenger of Allah to confirm his prophethood? As soon as the Messenger of Allah spoke, she affirmed him, stood beside him, strengthened him and calmed his fear, and said to him: "By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You join the ties of kinship, bear the burdens of others (tahmil al-kall)(3), and help in the calamities of time."(4)

The meaning of "mahjuran" (abandoned): from hajr, which is severing a relationship. If it is from one side only, it is hajr; if it is from both sides, it is hājara. The meaning is that they abandoned the Qur'an and cut off their connection with it, which means that they cut themselves off from divinity and cut themselves off from the Muhammadan message; they did not take the proofs of certain belief, they cut themselves off from the message when they denied it, and cut themselves off from the rulings when they disobeyed them. Thus they took this Qur'an as abandoned in all these matters: the creed, the acts of worship, and affirmation of the Messenger.

Yet if the Arabs had understood His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people...﴾ (43:44), they would have glorified the Qur'an and held fast to it, for it is what preserved them and preserved their language, and raised their renown among the nations. Had every contemporary nation taken its own particular national dialect and made it a language, Arabic as a language would have vanished.

In many countries of the Arab world, if they speak to you in their particular dialect, you understand nothing of it; and were it not for Classical Arabic, the language of the Qur'an, binding these dialects together, each would have become a separate language, as happened to the Latin languages from which French, Italian, German and English were born; each has its own foundations and rules, though they were originally one language, but they have no bond of a holy book.

Thus the Almighty alerts them that the Qur'an contains their remembrance, their honour and their might, and in it is their fame and renown. The Qur'an made the Arabs known on every tongue; without it they would have melted among the nations as nations and civilizations before them melted, of which no one has heard.

Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) says to them: "If you believe in what I have brought, it will be your share in this world and the Hereafter; and if you reject my word, I will be patient until Allah judges between me and you."(5)

(1) The poet is Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma, the wisest of the poets in the Jahiliyya. His father, his maternal uncle, his sister Sulma and his two sons Ka'b and Bujayr, and his sister al-Khansa', were all poets. He was born in the land of Muzayna in the vicinity of Madina, and his most famous poetry is his Mu'allaqa. He died in about 13 BH. (al-A'lam of al-Zirikli 3/52).
(2) Diwan of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma, 73, and Husn al-Tawassul, p. 231.
(3) Tahmil al-kall: that is, helping the burdened, and from it spending on the weak, the orphan and dependants. See al-Nawawi's commentary on Muslim (2/561) and Fath al-Bari of al-Asqalani (1/24).
(4) A hadith agreed upon (Muttafaq 'alayh), related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (3) and in six other places in his Sahih, and likewise by Muslim in his Sahih (160), from the hadith of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her.
(5) Mentioned by Ibn Hisham in al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (1/296) within the hadith of the delegation of the Quraysh disbelievers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 25, verse 31:

﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals. And sufficient is your Lord as a guide and a helper.﴾

If the Messenger had no enemies, why would he have come? If we expected everyone to believe in and affirm the Messenger the moment he arrived, then why would the Messenger have come? The Messenger only comes when corruption has spread and become general, just as we only bring in the doctor when an illness or an epidemic has struck.

These people had lordship and standing, and Islam came to level people equally and to strip these people of their dominance. So they were bound to take a stance of enmity towards it, and this enmity is the very reason for the Messenger's presence among them. The Prophet (ﷺ) was not unique in this: there was no prophet who did not have enemies, even though the earlier prophets were sent for a limited period of time and to a limited place.

As for the message of Muhammad (ﷺ), it was a message universal in time and in place, so the enmity must - therefore - be proportionate to the spread and universality of the message in time and place until the Hour arrives, and the Prophet (ﷺ) must prepare himself for that.

The word ʿaduww (عدو, "enemy") is one of the words that is used in the singular while including the dual and the plural. An example of this is His saying, on the tongue of our master Abraham: ﴿فإنهم عدو لي إلا رب العالمين﴾ (al-Shu'ara', 77). [Translator's note: the quotation reads "Indeed they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds."]

And in Surat al-Kahf: ﴿أفتتخذونه وذريته أولياء من دوني وهم لكم عدو...﴾ (al-Kahf, 50), and He did not say a'da'.

In some verses it comes in the plural form, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿واذكروا نعمت الله عليكم إذ كنتم أعداء فألف بين قلوبكم...﴾ (Al 'Imran, 103). So if it were purely a linguistic matter, it would have come in the singular form in all the verses.

But why did the Qur'an here shift from the singular form to the plural form?

They said: If the enmity, whether singular, dual or plural, is one single enmity, He says "ʿaduww" in the singular because the cause of the enmity is unified. But if the enmities are different: this one opposes you for your nobility, this one opposes you for your knowledge, this one opposes you for your wealth, and the causes of enmity multiply, He says "a'da'" (enemies). As for the matter of faith and certainty with regard to the disbelievers, the enmity is one, but in worldly affairs the enmities are many: this one opposes you for such-and-such, and that one opposes you for such-and-such, because he contradicts his desires.

And when we spoke of His saying: ﴿ولا على أنفسكم أن تأكلوا من بيوتكم أو بيوت آبائكم أو بيوت أمهاتكم...﴾ (al-Nur, 61), all of them are in the plural form except in His saying: ﴿أو صديقكم...﴾ (al-Nur, 61), in the singular form. Why? Because the friendship of believers ought to be for only one meaning, which is love for God and for the sake of God. It is not fitting for you to have a friend for such-and-such and another friend for such-and-such.

On this the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has three qualities will find the sweetness of faith: that God and His Messenger are dearer to him than anything else; that he loves a person only for God's sake; and that he hates to return to disbelief just as he hates to be thrown into the Fire." (1)

So if your friends love you for the sake of God, they are all like one friend.

And His saying: ﴿وكذلك...﴾ (al-Furqan, 31): meaning, like your enemies who took the Qur'an as something abandoned, and who took a stance towards you of obstinacy, harm and mockery.

﴿جعلنا لكل نبي عدوا من المجرمين...﴾ (al-Furqan, 31): that is, those who commit crimes, meaning those who perpetrate offences, which are acts of disobedience and sins according to their meanings.

When Allah, blessed and exalted is He, reveals to His Messenger (ﷺ) the reality of his enemies, that they are many and that they are criminals, it is only so that he prepares himself for that, so that he is not taken by surprise and endures their harm if they inflict any evil upon him. This matter is like the vaccine and immunization that people are given to confront disease before it occurs; Allah, exalted is He, gives His Messenger the immunity necessary to confront the enemies of the call.

For this reason we find that Churchill, the British leader who steered the Second World War, used to confront his soldiers with realities more horrible than they actually were, and whatever hardships he faced them with, he would tell them there was still more of them to come, so that when that happened they would be prepared for it.

And His saying: ﴿وكفى بربك هاديا ونصيرا﴾ (al-Furqan, 31): that is, Allah, exalted is He, will guide you to the path by which you will triumph over all of them. We have already mentioned about al-Faruq 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that when the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿سيهزم الجمع ويولون الدبر﴾ (al-Qamar, 45) was revealed, he said: "Which host is this?" meaning: he was amazed at how these people would be defeated while we are now unable even to protect ourselves, and we do not spend the night except armed, and we do not rise in the morning except armed, fearing that people will snatch us away. Then when Badr took place and the polytheists were defeated and the lives of their champions were reaped, he said: "Allah has spoken truly: ﴿سيهزم الجمع ويولون الدبر﴾" (al-Qamar, 45) (2).

How did this happen? It happened through Allah's guidance of His Messenger (ﷺ) to the causes of victory. Allah, blessed and exalted is He, grants victory to a thing and grants victory through its opposite. At Badr there gathered the chiefs of Quraysh, their strong and their wealthy, and the champions of disbelief in it, until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "This is Makkah; it has thrown to you the choicest pieces of its liver" (3) (4). They had all come out in a state of readiness for war, whereas the believers were a small and oppressed group, not prepared for war; yet Allah gave them victory.

Allah, exalted is He, reassures His Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers with him: ﴿كم من فئة قليلة غلبت فئة كثيرة بإذن الله...﴾ (al-Baqarah, 249).

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿وإن جندنا لهم الغالبون﴾ (al-Saffat, 173).

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿أولم يروا أنا نأتي الأرض ننقصها من أطرافها...﴾ (al-Ra'd, 41): that is, We diminish from the land of disbelief and increase in the land of faith. Allah, exalted is He, has informed us of matters which must bring about events in life and reality that serve to confirm these matters.

1 A hadith agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh), related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (16) and likewise Muslim in his Sahih (43), both in the Book of Faith, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him.

2 Ibn Kathir cited it in his Tafsir and attributed it to Ibn Abi Hatim (4/266), from 'Ikrimah, who said: "When the verse ﴿سيهزم الجمع ويولون الدبر﴾ (al-Qamar, 45) was revealed, 'Umar said: 'Which host will be defeated?' That is, which host will be overcome? 'Umar said: So when the day of Badr came, I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) leaping in his armour, saying: 'سيهزم الجمع ويولون الدبر', and I understood its interpretation on that day."

3 Al-fulzah: a piece of liver, flesh, wealth, gold or silver; its plural is afla'. In the hadith of Badr: "This is Makkah, it has thrown to you the choicest pieces of its liver," meaning the pure core of Quraysh, its essence and its nobles, as one says: "So-and-so is the heart of his tribe," because the liver is among the noblest organs (Lisan al-'Arab, root f-l-dh).

4 Related by al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-Nubuwwah (3/43), and cited by Ibn Hisham in al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah (2/617) from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr.

Then the Truthful One, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?" Thus [it is], that We may strengthen your heart thereby, and We have spaced it out in gradual recitation.﴾
