Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 25, verse 65:

﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell; indeed its punishment is ever-adhering (gharaman)."﴾:

This statement befits the servants of the Most Merciful, who do good deeds, hoping for reward and fearing punishment. It is they who say, ﴿Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell; indeed its punishment is ever-adhering (gharaman).﴾ (al-Furqan). The word (gharam) we use to mean love, passionate attachment, and ardent love, but its meaning here is: adherence (al-luzum), that is, it clings to them and never leaves them in the Fire, forever; because the outcome is either Paradise forever, or Fire forever.

So the meaning of ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-adhering (gharaman)﴾ (al-Furqan) is: constant and perpetual, not a single occurrence after which the matter ends.

From the same root is the word (al-gharim), the one who clings to the debtor to take his debt from him.

As for the phrase ﴿avert from us the punishment of Hell...﴾ (al-Furqan), it is as if they imagine that Hell will pursue them, and that between it and them there is a contention (ladd), as evidenced by its saying: ﴿Is there any more?﴾ (Qaf, 30).

Then the verses mention the reason for this statement: ﴿Indeed, it is evil as a settlement and a station.﴾

Evil (sā'a) means ugliness, and its opposite is goodness; for this reason, in contrast to this verse, Allah says about Paradise: ﴿Excellent it is as a place of settlement and a station﴾ (al-Furqan 76). Thus evil is accompanied by ugliness, and goodness is accompanied by goodness.

And He said: ﴿as a place of settlement and a station﴾ (al-Furqan 66), lest they think that the Fire is a period that comes to an end, after which they leave it. Rather, it is their permanent abode and their station from which they never depart.

Or, Allah—glorified and exalted be He—intended by this two types of people: a believer who transgressed in some of the sins and did not repent, or whose repentance Allah did not accept; he is in the Fire for a period, and "settlement" here means a temporary place, whereas "station" means the path.

So: people are evil as a settlement for one who transgressed against himself and did not repent, or whose repentance Allah did not accept; he is in the Fire for a period, and "settlement" here means a temporary place, whereas "station" means the lengthy one.

So: the Fire is evil as a settlement for one who transgressed against himself and did not repent, or whose repentance Allah did not accept; it is not a permanent residence, and "station" is for those who abide in it forever.

Then the Exalted says:

﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever a moderate way between that﴾ (67)

Al-israf (extravagance): squandering what you possess on things that yield no benefit. So we do not call "musrif" (extravagant), for example, the one who eats in order to preserve his life. This is why our master ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said to his son ʿAsim(1): "Eat half of your stomach, do not discard a garment until you have worn it out (istakhlaqtahu)(2), and do not make all your provision go into your belly and onto your body(3)."

Israf is to spend in what is not lawful. There is no extravagance in what is lawful. Even if a person is extravagant in some permissible luxury, he is providing for himself some non-essential comforts, while providing for society necessary things. The one who wears no garment except pressed (mukawiyan) could have worn it without ironing; so ironing the garment is, for him, a kind of luxury. Yet for the presser (al-mukawwaji) it is a necessity, since it earns him his livelihood.

And the one who takes a taxi when he is able to walk, or who sits at the coffee-house every day to have his shoes shined when he is able to shine them himself: all of these are kinds of luxury for you, but they are a necessity for others. So this is not called extravagance.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and between that is a moderate way﴾ (al-Furqan) means: between extravagance and stinginess. ﴿a moderate way﴾ (al-Furqan) means: a middle course, i.e., spending is a middle point between two extremes. The qiwam (support/standard) of a thing is that by which it stands, and all of life stands upon the process of balancing between extravagance and stinginess.

We recall, when we were students, that they taught us the theory of levers: how one centres a fulcrum on a wooden stick so that the two arms are equal, and they will be even, neither one tilting the other. If one of them wants to tilt, the other resists it, as if saying to it: "We are here." If you hang a weight on one of the arms, you must lengthen the other to counter that weight.

It is narrated that ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan(4), when he wished to marry his daughter Fatimah to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, tested him with this question to learn his balance in life: "O ʿUmar, what is your expenditure?" He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, my expenditure is good, between two bad things,"(5) and then he recited this verse: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever a moderate way between that﴾ (al-Furqan).

The caliph knew that his son-in-law walks a path that guarantees for him and his wife the necessities of life, and likewise guarantees the higher necessities of the soul and of society.

We have previously mentioned that the person who spends his entire income cannot elevate his life or the life of his children, because he has been extravagant in spending and has saved nothing to build, for example, a house, or to buy a car, and so on.

The calamity of society is greater in the case of stinginess. The interest of society is that you spend and that you save, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched...﴾ (29) (al-Isra').

Thus God has made for us a measure between extravagance and stinginess, because wealth is the support of life. The one who is stingy is stingy towards himself and towards people: he has no needs to purchase, by which he participates in the movement of life and benefits others. So for these goods, these industries, and these workers and craftsmen, from where would they then earn their living, if there is no consumption and circulation of their goods? There is no doubt that stinginess causes stagnation and causes unemployment, and these are among the most destructive diseases for society.

And if you look at a loaf of bread, which is the simplest of life's necessities, consider how many workers, craftsmen, farmers, engineers, mills, warehouses, factories and bakeries stand behind it. Suppose you refrained from it, for example: what would happen?

So your Lord wants you to spend some and save some, which enables you to achieve the advancement of your life and its ambitions. Therefore the preceding verse was concluded with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So you will sit reproached and destitute﴾ (29) (al-Isra').

Reproached (malum) in yourself for having squandered wealth from which your dependants did not benefit, and destitute (mahsuran) when you see that others have advanced in life while you have done nothing. So: a person is blameworthy if he is extravagant, and destitute if he is stingy, and the standard lies in the middle between the two, and in "the good between two bad things," as ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz (may Allah be pleased with him) said. That is why they said: "The best of matters is the middle one."

(1) He is ʿAsim ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab al-Qurashi al-ʿAdawi: a poet, who was among the best of people in character, tall and large of build. He was the maternal grandfather of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz. Born in 6 AH, died at al-Rabadha in 70 AH at the age of 65. (al-Aʿlam by al-Zirikli 3/248).
(2) Khalaqa al-thawb khulukan: it wore out; and shay' khalaq: worn out (Lisan al-ʿArab, root kh-l-q). ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) meant that he should not discard his son's garment until it became old and worn out.
(3) Mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (7/4951), where it reads: "and do not be of a people who place what Allah has provided for them in their bellies and on their backs." ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab was himself an example to his son in this, for Abu Nuʿaym narrated in al-Hilya (1/53) that al-Hasan al-Basri said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab addressed the people while he was caliph, wearing a waist-wrap with twelve patches...
(4) He is Abu al-Walid al-Umawi, one of the great caliphs and shrewdest of them. Born in Madina in 26 AH, he grew up there as a jurist of wide knowledge and devotion. Muʿawiya appointed him governor of Madina at the age of 16. In his time the registers (al-dawawin) were Arabicised, and letters were pointed with dots and vowel marks; he was the first to strike dinars in Islam and inscribe them in Arabic. He died in 86 AH at the age of 61. (al-Aʿlam 4/165).
(5) Mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (7/4951).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 25, verse 68:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:(1)

﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse. And whoever does that will meet a penalty.﴾ (68)

Here someone may ask: after all these attributes of the servants of the Most Merciful, why is this attribute negated of them, ﴿who do not invoke with Allah another god...﴾ (68) (al-Furqan), when they only possessed the previous attributes because they believe in the One God, glory be to Him? They said: this matter is a foundational creed which the Qur'an must repeat and give emphasis to.

The meaning of ﴿who do not invoke with Allah another god...﴾ (68) (al-Furqan) is: they do not invoke the possessors of causes for their effects. This is the hidden shirk (polytheism). From it is their saying: "I put my trust in Allah and in you." So we say to him: Be mindful, there is nothing upon me; the whole matter is up to Allah. So say: "I put my trust in Allah." And if you wish, say: "Then in you."(2)

And we hear another say about an important matter: "This is upon me, and the rest is upon Allah." He made the important principle his own and attributed the rest to Allah. Is this fitting, when the whole matter, its roots and branches, is with Allah?

So: this verse may be for those ensnared by causes, who expect giving from them and forget the Causer, glory be to Him, and this is the hidden shirk.

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right...﴾ (68) (al-Furqan). We have previously spoken of the difference between death and killing, and said: both take away life, but in death life departs first, then the structure collapses afterward; whereas in the case of killing, the structure collapses first, followed by the departure of the soul. So death is in the hand of Allah, mighty and majestic, while killing may be in the hand of humans.

Here is an explicit prohibition of this crime, because "cursed is he who demolishes the building of Allah" and destroys the life which Allah, exalted is He, has bestowed upon His servants.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except by right...﴾ (68) (al-Furqan) means: a right that permits killing, such as stoning the adulterer to death, retaliation against the murderer, and killing the apostate from his religion. If we kill these, we kill them on the basis of a right that required their killing.

If someone says: then where is freedom of religion? We say: you are free to believe or not to believe, but know first that if you apostatize from your faith, we will kill you. So beware of entering our religion except after complete conviction, lest you expose yourself to this consequence.

This condition constitutes an obstacle and barrier before one who wishes to believe, and makes him think carefully before he utters the word of faith and take precautions for himself. So your Lord, mighty and majestic, warns you first and stipulates for you; and no one may then say: where is the compulsion in religion?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not commit unlawful sexual intercourse...﴾ (68) (al-Furqan). We spoke about this matter at the beginning of Surat al-Nur, and said: the human being whom Allah honoured and made His vicegerent on His earth, He willed for him purity and dignity, and that he inhabit the world according to the law of Allah. Thus no element that contradicts this law enters into the vicegerency; because Allah, exalted is He, wills to build the believing society upon purity, and to build it upon the care of the educator for the one educated.

Therefore you find a man caring for his child with food, drink and clothing, and sacrificing himself for him. Why? Because he is his child from his loins and is reckoned to him. But if he doubts his child's lineage to him, he neglects him, and perhaps thinks of getting rid of him. And if such a one is raised as a foundling with no origin, this is not fit for the vicegerency of Allah on His earth, nor for bearing this honour.

This shows that sound human nature refuses that there exist in the creation of Allah a person not ascribed to his true father. From here Islam forbade fornication, and made it among the attributes of the servants of the Most Merciful that they do not commit adultery.

﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty.﴾ (68) (al-Furqan) "Athaman" is like "nakalan" and "zinan" in meaning; and "al-athām" is the punishment for sin and the recompense for it.

(1) Occasion of revelation of the verse: on the authority of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: Which sin is greatest? He said: That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you. He said: Then which? He said: That you kill your child lest he eat with you. He said: Then which? He said: That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife. Abdullah said: And Allah revealed in confirmation of that: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god...﴾ (68) (al-Furqan). Cited by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (3/326), al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (7/4952), and al-Wahidi in Asbab al-Nuzul (p. 192). The hadith is in the Two Sahihs of al-Bukhari and Muslim and the authors of the Sunan.

(2) Ibn Majah related in his Sunan (2117) from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If one of you swears, let him not say: 'Whatever Allah wills and you will,' but let him say: 'Whatever Allah wills, then you.'"

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 25, verse 69:

﴿Their punishment will be doubled for them on the Day of Resurrection, and they will abide therein in humiliation.﴾

How are we to understand the doubling of the punishment in this verse, given His saying in another verse: ﴿And the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it...﴾ (al-Shura: 40)?

And He, glorified is He, says: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times the like thereof; but whoever brings an evil deed will not be recompensed except with the like thereof, and they will not be wronged.﴾ (al-An'am: 160)

In truth, there is no contradiction between the verses of the Noble Qur'an. The one who commits this act becomes a model (uswah) in society, emboldening others to commit this crime. Therefore he bears its burden (wizr) as the doer first, and he bears the burden of whoever follows his example.

As He, the Exalted, says, relating the words of the disbelievers: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a way, and indeed we are following in their footsteps.﴾ (al-Zukhruf: 23). Thus, the presence of the fathers as a model of evil increases the evil of the sons, so it is as if they are partners in it.

For this reason He, the Exalted, says in another place: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and [also] some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge...﴾ (al-Nahl: 25)

And He says: ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens...﴾ (al-'Ankabut: 13)

The first burden is for their own misguidance in itself, and the other burden is because they misled others. This is the meaning of the doubling of the punishment.

As for His saying, ﴿and abide therein in humiliation﴾ (al-Furqan: 69), the meaning of (muhanan) (humiliated): when the Qur'an describes the punishment, it describes it once as painful (alim), once as great (azim), and once as humiliating (muhin). The one who looks at the pain of the limbs says: this is a painful punishment, because it pains every part of the body. Punishment is a sensory matter, whereas humiliation is a matter of the inner self. Some people are pained by a single word that touches their dignity, while others are struck and are not affected by it.

The Creator, Mighty and Majestic, created people and knew from eternity that they are children of changing states (aghyar), that none of them is free from fault except the Messengers. Therefore, evil is possible from them.

And among the perfection of His mercy, as the Lord, is that He opened the door of repentance for His servants, for whoever of them has transgressed against himself in something, because the one who commits an evil, if he despairs of forgiveness, its danger spreads and its corruption increases. But if the door of repentance and forgiveness is opened for him, he returns to the right path, stands firm in obedience, and in this there is mercy for the whole society.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on surah 25, verse 70:

He says, may He be exalted:

﴿Except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds; for those, Allah will replace their misdeeds with good deeds. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (25:70)

Your Lord is Generous and Merciful. So if you advance righteous deeds and your regret grows strong over what you missed of disobedience, He will replace your misdeeds with good deeds.

Repentance (tawbah) has two aspects: its legislation (mashru'iyyah) comes from Allah first, and its acceptance comes from the one who repents second. Its legislation is a favour, and its acceptance is another favour. For this reason He, glorified is He, says: ﴿Then He turned to them in order that they might repent...﴾ (9:118). The meaning is: He turned to them by prescribing repentance for them, so that they would not be ashamed of returning to Allah.

As for His saying: ﴿Except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds...﴾ (25:70), "repent and believe" applies to one who has committed a sin that takes him out of faith. The disobedient person does not commit the sin except in heedlessness of his faith, as the noble hadith states: "The adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer, and the wine-drinker does not drink wine while he is a believer."¹

If the disobedient person were to keep the majesty of his Lord in mind, he would not disobey Him; the sin would loom large in his eyes and he would turn away from it. Since his faith has departed from him, he must renew it, and then employ this faith in righteous deeds.

﴿Except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds...﴾ (25:70), so the recompense is ﴿for those, Allah will replace their misdeeds with good deeds...﴾ (25:70). It is not meant that the misdeed is transformed directly into a good deed. Rather, the servant lifts the misdeed and repentance takes its place, and after repentance Allah records a good deed for him.

The mercy and forgiveness of Allah have emboldened some people, to the point that a poet said:
"My Master, I have disobeyed You deliberately,
yet You are most beautiful when You pardon.
I have gathered sins, the greatest of them,
yet I am loath that Your pardon should be small."

Some people have reached the point of multiplying misdeeds, hoping they will be turned into good deeds. But who guarantees him that he will live until he repents, or that if he repents, Allah will accept it from him?

The psychological cause that the scholars spoke of regarding this matter is that one who has stayed far from sin and has not fallen into its snares has not tasted the pleasure of desire, so it does not occur to his mind. As for one who has plunged into it, tasted its pleasure, and excessively indulged himself in it, he suffers greatly when he restrains himself and keeps himself away from disobedience to Allah. It is this suffering that has earned him this rank.

¹ A hadith agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh). Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (2475), and likewise Muslim in his Sahih (57), Kitab al-Iman, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 25, verse 71:

﴿And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, then indeed he turns back to Allah with a (sincere) turning back.﴾

The meaning of ﴿يتوب إلى الله متابا﴾ (al-Furqan 25:71) is: a sincere repentance (tawbah nasuhan), with no return after it to disobedience. He does not go back on his repentance like one who mocks his Lord, who says, "I will do such-and-such, then I will repent." The word ﴿متابا﴾ means: the resolve, at the moment of repenting, that he will not return (to sin). The danger lies in a servant committing a sin while counting on repentance being available, for he may be seized in the state of disobedience before he is able to repent.(1)

(1) Al-Qaffal said: It is possible that the first verse refers to those among the polytheists who repent, which is why He said, ﴿except for one who repents and believes... 70﴾ (al-Furqan). Then He conjoined to it those Muslims who repent and follow their repentance with righteous deeds, so they too have the ruling of those who repent. (Tafsir al-Qurtubi, 7/4956).

Then the verses mention another of the qualities of the servants of the Most Merciful:

﴿And those who do not bear witness to falsehood, and when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity.﴾ (25:72)

Al-zūr (falsehood): a false thing; one "yazūr" in testimony, i.e., establishes a right for someone other than its owner. But we note that the verse did not say "those who do not bear witness to falsehood (bi-l-zūr)", which indicates that the verse has a broader meaning than merely uttering false statements in the domain of litigation, where one says of a judge: "So-and-so did such-and-such, when he did not do it."

So "shahādah" (witnessing) has another meaning: namely, not attending falsehood. Al-zūr is everything that opposes the truth, and among its uses is the saying of the Exalted in regard to the month of Ramadan: ﴿Whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it...﴾ (2:185).

So the meaning of ﴿they do not bear witness to falsehood﴾ (25:72) is: they do not attend falsehood in any of its forms, whether in speech, action, or acquiescence, and everything that opposes the truth.

Therefore the Exalted says elsewhere: ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say: "For us our deeds and for you your deeds; peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant."﴾ (28:55)

And He, glorified, says: ﴿And if Satan causes you to forget, then do not sit after the reminder with the wrongdoing people.﴾ (6:68)

And the Exalted said: ﴿And it has already been revealed to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being rejected and mocked, do not sit with them until they enter into a conversation other than that...﴾ (4:140).

It is well known that uttering falsehood and bearing false witness overturn realities and harm society; for when you bear false witness, you take the right from its owner and give it to another, and this leads to the paralysis of the movement of life, and makes a person feel insecure about the fruits of his toil and sweat, so people refrain from striving and working, as long as the matter in the end is falsehood.

Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins? Associating partners with Allah, disobedience to parents, and false witness." The Prophet (ﷺ) was reclining, then sat up, and he kept repeating it until we said: "I wish he would be silent." [1]

Why? Because false witness destroys all cases of truth in society.

Then He, glorified, says: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ (25:72). Al-laghw (idle talk): that which, in the estimation of the intelligent person, should be nullified and abandoned; it is the babble that has no benefit. Therefore He said of those who abandon it: ﴿they pass by with dignity﴾ (25:72). The "karām" (dignified/noble) is contrasted with the "li'ām" (base/vile), so the meaning is: do not enter with the base into the domain of idle talk and false speech that collides with the truth in order to turn people away from it.

Among that is what the Qur'an relates about the disbelievers, who wanted to turn people away from listening to the verses of the Reminder: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it...﴾ (41:26).

That is: create confusion around it so that people cannot hear it. This is a testimony from them that if they left people's ears in their natural state, they would hear the Qur'an, and would inevitably be benefited by it and believe in it; and if the Qur'an had no effect on souls, they would not have said this statement.

Their saying ﴿and make noise during it﴾ (41:26) means: if you hear it being recited, then make noise during it and confuse it, so that it does not reach the ears. Why? Did not our master 'Umar embrace Islam when he heard verses from it in the house of his sister Fatimah? But why did the Qur'an affect 'Umar this time in particular, when he had heard it many times without being affected by it?

They said: because obstinacy and stubbornness make a person hear as one who does not hear. As for 'Umar's hearing this time, it was after he struck his sister and split her head, and blood flowed from her; this stirred in him the feeling of brotherhood and its tenderness, and shook off from him pride, obstinacy, and contentiousness. So the Qur'an encountered in him a pure soul and a heart free of hostility (lidd) toward Islam, and he embraced Islam.

Do you not see the disbelievers, some of whom say to others upon hearing the Qur'an, as the Qur'an relates: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, until when they leave your presence they say to those who were given knowledge: "What did he just say?"...﴾ (47:16).

That is: what is the meaning of what he says? Or: what is the novelty he has brought? This is said in a manner of their astonishment. The Qur'an responds: ﴿Say: It is for those who believe a guidance and a healing; and those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is blindness upon them...﴾ (41:44).

So the Qur'an is one, but its reception differs: this one received it with a pure, content soul, and that one received it with stubborn hostility (lidd) and a closed heart, as if he had not heard it. The matter is one of action and of that which receives action. We previously illustrated this with someone who blows on his hands on cold winter days for warmth, and blows on a cup of tea, for example, to cool it: the action is one, but the reception differs.

[1] Recorded by Muslim in his Sahih (87), Kitab al-Iman, and Ahmad in his Musnad (5/37), and al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (3019), from the hadith of Abu Bakrah Nufay' ibn al-Harith. al-Tirmidhi said: this is a hasan gharib sahih hadith.
[2] al-Lidd: fierce contention; al-Aladd: one who is extremely contentious and argumentative. (Lisan al-'Arab, root l-d-d.)

**Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 25, verse 73:**

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord, do not fall down before them deaf and blind.﴾ (25:73)

The words of the Exalted, ﴿when they are reminded (dhukkiru)...﴾ (25:73), are not said except when the one you are reminding has familiarity with the reminder and knowledge of it. The signs by which one is reminded have a first appearance and a second appearance. The first appearance is the first proclamation of them; the second appearance is when one forgets, and so we remind you of them.

We have previously said that the word "signs" (ayat) is applied to three meanings: either cosmic signs that draw attention to the power of God, the Exalted, and that He is a wise Maker... etc.; or miraculous signs that came to support the messengers and establish their truthfulness in conveying from God; or the signs of the Wise Reminder (al-Dhikr al-Hakim), which are called bearers of rulings, and which awaken from heedlessness and remind people.

So the meaning of ﴿those who, when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord...﴾ (25:73), that is, in the Noble Qur'an: ﴿do not fall down before them deaf and blind.﴾ (25:73) "Do not fall down" (lam yakhirru): the *kharr* is falling without order and without arrangement.

As in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So God came at their structure from the foundations, and the roof fell down on them from above them...﴾ (16:26). So the roof, if it falls, falls without order and without arrangement.

From this is His saying, the Exalted, concerning the attributes of the believers: ﴿And they say, "Glory be to our Lord, indeed the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled." And they fall down upon their faces weeping...﴾ (17:108–109), because they fall down in a compelled emotional state arising from hearing the Qur'an.

Therefore: when they are reminded of the signs of God, they do not fall down before them deaf and blind; rather, they fall down while listening with complete attentiveness, and seeing with complete clarity.

Then the Almighty says:

﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and offspring the coolness of our eyes, and make us leaders for the righteous."﴾

This is another attribute of the servants of the Most Merciful. In it they ask for two things: ﴿Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and offspring the coolness of our eyes...﴾ Offspring come only after marriage, which is why the supplication mentions the spouses first and then the offspring.

The word ﴿qurrah...﴾ is used with two meanings. In the language there is what they call (ishtiqaq 'amil) (the common root derivation), meaning that a word is derived from a general meaning, and its sense may differ, but in the end the two meet in one meaning.

The word (qurrah) comes with the meaning of constancy and steadiness, from qarra fi al-makan, meaning he stayed in the place and settled in it; and it comes with the meaning of joy. Al-qarr also means intense cold, as in the verse of the poet:

Kindle the fire, for the night is a cold night,
and the wind is a wind that bites; so who will see your fire passing by?
If you bring a guest, then you are free.

So al-qarr is cold, and al-qarur is stillness, and a cool eye is a sign of joy, while a hot eye is a sign of sorrow and pain, in the words of the poet:

As for the hearts of the lovers, they were heated,
but as for the hearts of those who turn away (1), they were cooled.

Therefore they use coolness of the eye as an expression for joy and heat of the eye as an expression for sorrow. They say: "God gave me a son in whom my eye found coolness," and they say: "God heated the eye of so-and-so," meaning: He afflicted him with a grief from which his eye boils.

Since the eye is a precious jewel in the human body, the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, has surrounded it with special care and preserved for it in the body a suitable temperature that differs from the body's temperature, which is balanced at 37. Were the eye to take on that degree, it would burst.

Among the wonders of God's power is that the temperature of the eye is nine degrees, and the temperature of the liver is forty, and both are in one body.

So the meaning of ﴿the coolness of our eyes...﴾ is: make for us from our spouses what gladdens us, as in the noble hadith about the qualities of the righteous wife: "The believer has gained nothing better after fear of God than a righteous wife: if he orders her, she obeys him; if he looks at her, she delights him; if he swears an oath concerning her, she fulfils it for him; and if he is absent from her, she guards him in herself and his wealth" (2).

And grant us from our offspring children who are committed to God's method, who do not deviate from it, and who do not burden us beyond what we can bear in word or deed; for if a child comes contrary to this form, it is a great calamity to his parents. The proof is that a man may waste himself in various sins and fall short in the right of God, yet he grieves if his child does the same as he does.

The father may not pray, yet he urges his son to pray, and rejoices for him if he prays and goes straight. Why? Because he wants to see, and to compensate in his son for the good and beauty he himself missed. A person does not like to see another better than himself except his own child, for the child is his extension and his compensation for what has passed.

If we take ﴿the coolness of our eyes...﴾ to mean steadiness and constancy, the meaning is that the wife should have good character, manners and beauty, such that she pleases her husband, so that his eye does not reach out to others, and he settles with her because she has fulfilled all the conditions. Among that is the Exalted's saying: ﴿Do not extend your eyes toward what We have given enjoyment to some pairs of them...﴾ (al-Hijr 15:88).

Likewise, if he finds the qualities of goodness, manners and beauty in his children, such that his eye does not reach beyond them, for he sees in his children all his aspirations and everything he wishes for, so he does not look to others. That is why, when they praise someone, they say: "So-and-so no longer has any aspirations." Why? Because he has achieved all that he wanted.

They also say in praise: "So-and-so has fixed the gaze," meaning: when you see him, your eye settles on him and does not turn away from him, because of his beauty and the perfection of his qualities.

When a child is in this form, he gives his parents rest in this world and in the Hereafter, for he is a righteous child whose dutifulness to his parents does not end with their death; rather he remains dutiful to them even after death, supplicating for them. In the Hereafter, God will gather them all together in the abode of His mercy: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith — We will join with them their offspring...﴾ (al-Tur 52:21).

Thus all of this, in spouses and in children, is a gift and a bestowal from God.

We observe that some spouses live with their partners reluctantly, and perhaps with aversion, which the circumstances of life, the children and the stability of the household compel them to bear. If you tell the husband: "Your wife will be with you in Paradise," he says: "How? Even in the Hereafter?!" He does not know that God, exalted is He, will purify her of the qualities he disliked in her in this world.

He, glorified is He, says: ﴿For those who are mindful of God there are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pure spouses...﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:15).

And He says: ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joy, they and their spouses, in shade, reclining upon couches﴾ (Ya Sin 36:55–56).

As for His saying: ﴿and make us leaders for the righteous﴾ — we observe that the supplication here is collective, yet He did not say "imams" (a'immah) but mentioned "imam" in the singular. Why?

They said: because He, exalted is He, alerts us that the imam is the one who walks according to God's method and does not deviate from it; therefore, if the imams are many, they are all under the ruling of one imam, because they proceed from one Lord and one method, not governed by whims that would scatter them like princes, for example. So He unified them in speech — each of them individually — and made them one in leadership.

(1) Izal al-shay' yaʻzilhu fa-i'tazalahu: he set it aside, so it withdrew. (Lisan al-'Arab, root ʻ-z-l). That is, they removed their hearts from passion, from desire and from union, so their hearts rested and became settled.

(2) Related by Ibn Majah in his Sunan (1857) from the hadith of Abu Umamah, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Busiri said in his Zawa'id: "In its chain is ʻAli ibn Yazid. Al-Bukhari said: he is munkar al-hadith. ʻUthman ibn Abi al-ʻAtikah is disputed. The hadith was related by al-Nasa'i from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and he remained silent about it. It has a witness from the hadith of Ibn ʻUmar."

(3) Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (1/352): "That is, purified from filth, impurity, harm, menstruation, postnatal bleeding and other things that afflict the women of this world." Ibn Manzur in Lisan al-'Arab (root: t-h-r) quoted Abu Ishaq on the meaning of this word in the verse: "Its meaning is that they do not need what the women of this world need after eating and drinking, they do not menstruate, and they do not need anything to purify themselves with; and yet they are pure with the purity of character and chastity. So 'mutahharah' gathers all purity, because 'mutahharah' is more eloquent in speech than 'tahirah.'"

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 25, verse 75:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, speaks about the reward of the servants of the Most Merciful:

﴿Those will be rewarded with the high chamber (1) for their patience, and they will be met therein with greeting and peace.﴾ (75)

﴿Those...﴾ (75) (al-Furqan) is a report about the servants of the Most Merciful whose attributes have already been mentioned. Their reward is ﴿they will be rewarded with the high chamber...﴾ (75) (al-Furqan). The word "chamber" (al-ghurfah) comes in the singular, although they are many, and each one of them needs a chamber of his own.

They said: this is because al-ghurfah here means the lofty place which contains many chambers, as the Exalted said: ﴿But whoever believes and does righteousness, those will have the double reward for what they did, and they will be secure in the chambers﴾ (37) (Saba').

This reward is the result of ﴿for their patience...﴾ (75) (al-Furqan): they were patient over the hardships of acts of obedience. The Prophet (ﷺ) clarified this matter when he said: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and the Fire is surrounded by desires" (2).

So Paradise requires that I be patient over the hardships of acts of obedience, that I estimate the reward for the deed and keep it present in my mind in the Hereafter. If I grow weary of acts of obedience and deny the reward of the Hereafter, then why act at all?

We illustrate this with the student who studies diligently and strives in his lessons, because he keeps the day of the examination and its result in mind, and how his position will be on that day. Thus: if a person keeps the reward for obedience in mind, its hardships become easy and light for him, and if he keeps in mind the consequence of disobedience and what awaits him of its punishment, he will keep away from it.

Religious obligations thus require patience, as the Exalted said: ﴿And seek help in patience and prayer, and indeed it is difficult except for the humble﴾ (45) (al-Baqarah).

The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, wants us not to separate obligations from their reward; rather, place the reward before your eyes before you proceed to the deed.

For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) asked one of his companions: "How did you wake up, O Harithah?" (3) He replied: "I woke up a true believer." He said: "Every truth has a reality; what is the reality of your faith?"

He said: "My soul has turned away from this world, so that gold and clay are alike to it, and it is as if I look at the people of Paradise in Paradise enjoying bliss, and at the people of the Fire in the Fire being tormented."

So the matter, then, in their view was not unseen but witnessed, as if they saw it from the intensity of their certainty. Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "You have known, so hold fast" (5).

And Imam Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, said: "Even if the veil were lifted from me, I would not increase in certainty." Why? Because he had reached in certainty the level of knowledge and direct witnessing.

Then the Exalted says: ﴿and they will be met therein with greeting and peace﴾ (75) (al-Furqan).

Greeting (tahiyyah): that we say to him, "We greet you," meaning: we wish you life, by your being at ease with us. Peace (salam): safety and mercy. But from whom is the peace? The word "peace" (salam) occurs in the Noble Qur'an with three meanings:

Peace from Allah, as in His saying: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ (58) (Ya-Sin).

Peace from the angels: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, (23) "Peace be upon you..." (24)﴾ (al-Ra'd).

Peace from the people of al-A'raf, who are a people whose good deeds and bad deeds were equal, so they did not enter Paradise, nor did they enter the Fire; and these say: ﴿And upon the heights are men who recognize each by his mark, and they call out to the companions of Paradise, "Peace be upon you." They have not entered it, but they hope﴾ (46) (al-A'raf).

So: the servants of the Most Merciful will be met in Paradise with peace from Allah, peace from the angels, and peace from the people of al-A'raf.

(1) al-Ghurfah: the high rank, which is the highest and most excellent of the abodes of Paradise, just as the ghurfah is the highest of the dwellings of this world. Related by Ibn Shajarah. Al-Dahhak said: al-Ghurfah is Paradise. (Mentioned by al-Qurtubi, 7/4961.)
(2) Related by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad (3/153-254), Muslim in his Sahih (2822), and al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (2559), from the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him.
(3) He is al-Harith ibn Malik al-Ansari; see his biography in "al-Isabah fi Tamyiz al-Sahabah" (1475) by Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, which mentions many narrations of this hadith.
(4) al-Madr: pieces of dried clay. (Lisan al-Arab, root: m-d-r.)
(5) Cited by al-Haythami in Majma' al-Zawa'id (1/57), who attributed it to al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, and said: "In it is Ibn Lahi'ah, and in it is one who needs to be examined."

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿Abiding therein forever; how excellent a place of settlement and station!﴾ (25:76)

It has already been mentioned that He said about Hell: ﴿How evil a place of settlement and station!﴾ (25:66), because it is ugly; and its counterpart here is ﴿how excellent...﴾ (25:76). Al-mustaqarr (المستقر) is the place of temporary, non-permanent sojourn, and al-maqam (المقام) is the place of permanent dwelling. It is well known that whoever enters Paradise dwells there in an everlasting, eternal abode.

As for whoever enters Hell, he may leave it if he is a believer. So how did He say of each of them: "mustaqarr and maqam"?

They said: Because at every moment there comes to them a bliss and a reward, we say to them: this is not the everlasting bliss. The mustaqarr is one blessing, whereas the maqam is in many other blessings, ascending and rising higher, to the degree that the perfections of Allah's bounty are without end.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, concludes Surat al-Furqan with His saying:

﴿Say: "My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication. But you have denied, so it will be inevitable."﴾

After the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, spoke of the servants of the Most Merciful, mentioned their attributes and their recompense, He turned to others who did not possess these qualities and for whom none of this bliss will be attained. He says to them: Beware lest you think that God, exalted is He, will concern Himself with you, or take heed of you, or be at your aid; for God, exalted is He, takes heed only of His servants who worshipped Him with the worship due to Him and obeyed Him with the obedience due to Him. You, on the other hand, have opposed the fundamental principle of the creation of beings, and you have not realized the meaning of vicegerency on earth, for which God, exalted is He, created you.

Just as you turned away from the way of God, paid it no heed, did not worship Him, and He was not in your minds, so too God does not care for you, you will not be mindful of Him, glory be to Him, and He will surely abandon you.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Were it not for your supplication...﴾ means: were it not for your worship, which has not occurred. ﴿...But you have denied...﴾ i.e., the fundamental principle, which is that you were created for worship. ﴿...so it will be inevitable﴾ — just as you persisted in disbelief in Me and did not worship Me, and you insisted upon disbelief, so likewise the recompense, being of the same kind as the deed, will be inevitable for you, and it will never leave you.
